briefing:
Mock interviewer: Hi, thanks for joining. Today we will design a URL shortening service, like bit.ly. Where would you like to start?

[[step: 1]]

interview.text:
Mock interviewer: Good start. Before we draw anything: how many users do we expect, and how many redirects per short link? Ask me for any number you need.

[[step: 1]]
[[covered: 1]]

Mock interviewer: Those numbers work. Give me a rough QPS estimate from them, and the storage per year. Feel free to round aggressively.

[[step: 1]]

Mock interviewer: About right, and I accept the rounding. Now sketch the high-level design: what sits between the user and the database?

[[step: 2]]
[[covered: 2]]

Mock interviewer: Clean sketch. Which piece is the hardest to get right at this scale? Walk me through its internals.

[[step: 3]]
[[covered: 3]]

Mock interviewer: Solid internals. What breaks first when traffic spikes tenfold? Name the bottlenecks.

[[step: 4]]
[[covered: 4]]

Mock interviewer: Good. Last part: how does this scale past one datacenter? Think data partitioning and availability.

[[step: 5]]
[[covered: 5]]

Mock interviewer: That covers the five steps. We can go deeper on any part, or you can ask to wrap up.

[[step: 5]]

ladder: Mock interviewer: Hint: read traffic dwarfs write traffic here by two orders of magnitude. What does that suggest?
Mock interviewer: Fuller answer: because reads dominate, put a cache in front of the key-value store and serve redirects mostly from it.

Mock interviewer: Walkthrough: a redirect request hits a load balancer, then a stateless redirect service, then the cache, then the KV store; the write path goes through an encoder service with a counter or hash plus collision check.
help.refusal: Mock interviewer: In testing mode I hold back hints. Try the numbers yourself and tell me what you get.

wrapup:
Mock interviewer: Time is up, thank you. That is a wrap on the exercise; the grade will follow shortly.

[[step: 5]]

rows.name: redundancy
rows.fix: Add a replica for the KV store and a load balancer pair; single instances are points of failure.

rows.name: queues
rows.fix: Move the alias-creation analytics path behind a queue so the write path stays thin.

rows.name: monitoring
rows.fix: Define redirect latency and cache hit ratio metrics with alert thresholds.

realism.note: Matches 100M DAU x 5 redirects / 86,400, within one order of magnitude.
Matches 10M records/day at ~300 bytes, friendly rounding accepted.

missing: Cache TTL was never stated for the redirect cache.
No discussion of hot key (popular alias) mitigation.

artifact_comments.comment: The diagram is clean; label the cache as cache-aside and add the replica.

grade.closing: Mock interviewer: Thanks, that is a solid pass with a few operational gaps. Good luck out there.

summarize.narrative: The candidate asked about scale. The interviewer answered 100 million reads per day. The candidate chose one database and a read cache in front of it.
decisions: A read cache in front of the database
estimates: About 1157 reads per second, from 100 million reads per day

grade_bad: I thought the design was quite good overall, though the caching story was thin.

obvious_gaps: No estimates yet: QPS and storage are still guesses.
The high-level sketch has not been drawn.
midgrade.note: This is a progress check only: the interview is still open.
